title: Byzantine-Robust Aggregation for Securing Decentralized Federated Learning

C-a.quote: WFAgg comprises three multipurpose filters, including a distance-based filter, a similarity-based filter, and a temporal-based filter.
C-a.locator: §IV; the composition is sequential and joint within one round -- "Since the filters operate sequentially and share intermediate model statistics, the overall cost increases only linearly with the number of filters" (§IV) -- and the fourth stage is the aggregator, whose purpose is also stated as defense: "The WFAgg-E algorithm is proposed as a model aggregation algorithm similar to the FedAvg ... This aggregation algorithm is designed for adversarial environments so that if a malicious model is selected for aggregation, its influence is mitigated" (§IV-F). Algorithm 1 shows the four stages in order: T1 = WFAgg-D(T, f), T2 = WFAgg-C(T, f), T3 = WFAgg-T(T, W, Tth), then the weighting and WFAgg-E(T, alpha, {w_ij})

C-b.quote: each filter using various well-known techniques in this field for mitigating or eliminating malicious models. This approach seeks to compensate for the inadequacies of some techniques in detecting specific attacks by leveraging other techniques.
C-b.locator: §I / §IV; the acceptance rule's reason is stated separately and is a constituent-vulnerability reason, "Considering that the algorithm may be attacked by targeting specific characteristics of some filters, it is understandable that a model must be accepted by two or more filters to be considered benign. This design decision is also influenced by the temporal-based filter, as it, by considering only temporal statistics, might identify a constan[t]" (§IV)

C-c.quote: Table I presents a general comparison of the robust aggregation schemes mentioned, by analyzing the accuracy metric in the testset, exposed to different poisoning attacks.
C-c.locator: §VI; the metric is the assembled scheme's own robust accuracy, with R-squared as a secondary (Fig. 6, "Comparison of R-Squared, R2, metric (last rou[nd])"), under No Attack / Noise / LF / SF / IPM-0.5 / IPM-100 / ALIE in both centralized and decentralized topologies

C-d.quote: evaluate and compare the single proposed algorithms of this paper in order to highlight their improvements and drawbacks compared to the state-of-the-art ones. Those algorithms are: WFAgg-D, WFAgg-C, WFAgg-T and WFAgg-E.
C-d.locator: §VI; WFAgg-E is the downstream aggregator, defined in Algorithm 1 as a function of the upstream filters' output weights, WFAgg-E(T, alpha, {w_ij}), and it is evaluated BOTH standalone and behind the filter stage (Fig. 6's panels are WFAgg-D, WFAgg-C, WFAgg-T, WFAgg-E, Alt-WFAgg, WFAgg), with alpha = 0.8 fixed throughout: "For the WFAgg-E algorithm, the smoothing factor is set to alpha = 0.8." A second instance in the same paper substitutes an upstream filter with the aggregator fixed, and the paper reads the outcome off that substitution: "the Alt-WFAgg algorithm achieves good results, only compromising its performance under the Noise attack. This is mainly due to the influence of the Clustering algorithm (which was unable to converge under this attack)" (§VI)

C-e.quote: This is mainly due to the influence of the Clustering algorithm (which was unable to converge under this attack).
C-e.locator: §VI, attributing Alt-WFAgg's single failure to a named upstream constituent; a second attributional claim about an attack class is at §VI, "worsen the results compared to the scenario without attacks. coder_note:
C-d = YES ON THE CLEANEST STRUCTURAL GROUNDS IN THE FRAME, AND THE DECIDING FACT WAS ALMOST MISSED. On a first reading this looked like three PARALLEL filters combined by a vote, in which case evaluating one filter alone would delete the >=2-of-3 acceptance rule and therefore change the downstream -- a leave-one-out, which the rubric explicitly excludes, the same trap CrowdGuard's Table V and G2uardFL's Table 10 set. Two sentences settle it the other way. First, the filters are SEQUENTIAL, not parallel: "Since the filters operate sequentially and share intermediate model statistics." Second, and decisively, Algorithm 1 declares the aggregator as WFAgg-E(T, alpha, {w_ij}) -- the downstream stage is literally a function whose argument is the upstream stage's output weights, with its own parameter alpha pinned at 0.8 in every arm. Evaluating WFAgg-E standalone and then WFAgg (filters feeding the same alpha = 0.8 aggregator) holds the downstream mechanism fixed and varies only the upstream input. That is the rubric's contrast in its strictest possible form: not a substitution, not an ablation of a peer, but the same downstream function called with a different upstream argument.

The paper supplies a SECOND, independent C-d instance in Alt-WFAgg, which swaps an upstream filter for a clustering-based one with the aggregator unchanged, and then attributes the resulting failure to the substituted component by name. So this row would code C-d = YES on either instance alone, and rule 4's benefit of the doubt is not needed for either.

WHY C-a = YES INCLUDES THE AGGREGATOR, WHICH MATTERS BECAUSE IT IS ALSO THE C-d ANCHOR. Amendment 3's purpose test is satisfied for WFAgg-E explicitly -- "designed for adversarial environments so that if a malicious model is selected for aggregation, its influence is mitigated" -- so it is a defense stage and not merely the averaging step every FL system has. Had it been plain FedAvg the C-a count would still reach three on the filters, so the code does not depend on this, but the C-d reading does depend on WFAgg-E being a stage with a fixed identity, which the alpha = 0.8 declaration supplies.

C-b IS THE SECOND-STRONGEST PAIRING REASON IN THE FRAME AFTER LASA'S, AND IT IS OF A THIRD KIND. BRFL's reason was cost complementarity; LASA's was matched threat complementarity with both halves quoted; this paper's is ADVERSARIAL complementarity -- the pairing exists because an attacker who targets the characteristics of one filter is caught by another, which is why acceptance requires two of three. C-b's frozen text admits it under "cover complementary threats or complementary regions of the attack space", and the quotation shows the reason rather than the fact of the pairing. A5's prose should record that the pairing reasons found in this literature are of at least three kinds; the pre-registration anticipated only two.

THE SCREENING TAGS WERE RIGHT HERE. Unlike SPFL's 'reputation' tag and refined-Krum's 'secure-agg' tag, both false positives, this paper's multi-filter tag is accurate and the composition is real.

EXTRACTOR NOTE: the C-d bucket did not surface either instance. The standalone-versus-composed comparison is announced as "evaluate and compare the single proposed algorithms of this paper", and Alt-WFAgg appears only as a figure-panel label and one prose sentence; neither uses ablation or component vocabulary. This is the fourth paper where the C-d bucket missed the sentence the code rests on, and the third distinct framing that defeats it (configuration list, parameter table, and now a comparison of the authors' own single algorithms). A5 discloses all four.
